title: UKBI — the proficiency test
goal: Know what the UKBI (Uji Kemahiran Berbahasa Indonesia) tests and how it grades, and master the two *kaidah* traps it loves most: the sentence with no subject and the redundant phrase.
bekal: spot and fix a subjectless sentence: *Dalam rapat itu membahas… → Rapat itu membahas…*
cut redundancy (*pleonasme*): *saling tolong-menolong, sangat … sekali, agar supaya*
talk about a test and its result: *skor, nilai, predikat, hasilnya keluar*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Latihan soal kaidah
dialogs.intro: Early November 2029. Sarah has registered for the UKBI at the Badan Bahasa in Rawamangun, East Jakarta. On a Saturday morning Dr. Lestari works through a practice paper with her at a campus café.

lines.literal: we start from section rule, [ya]. sentence this right or wrong: “in meeting that discuss budget year front.”

lines.text: Tentu. Coba cari subjeknya.

lines.text: “Rapat itu”? Oh, tidak bisa, karena didahului kata “dalam”. Jadi kalimatnya tidak bersubjek.

notes: **Kaidah** — rule, norm; *kaidah bahasa* is grammar in the prescriptive sense, the rules in the official guides. The UKBI section called *Merespons Kaidah* asks you to judge and correct sentences, and it is where educated native speakers lose the most points.

**Kalimat tidak bersubjek.** In Indonesian a noun preceded by a preposition (*dalam, di, bagi, menurut, dengan*) cannot be the subject. *Dalam rapat itu membahas…* therefore has an active verb and no one doing it. Everyday speech tolerates this all the time; the test does not.

**Atau pakai pasif.** The second fix is elegant: keep *dalam rapat itu* as a setting and make the verb passive, so that *anggaran* becomes the subject: *Dalam rapat itu dibahas anggaran*. A passive verb can come before its subject in Indonesian, which is why this sounds natural.

**Mubazir** — "wasteful", borrowed from Arabic, and the word teachers use for redundant words. The technical term is *pleonasme*. *Tolong-menolong* is already reciprocal, like *pukul-memukul* or *kunjung-mengunjungi*, so *saling* adds nothing.

**Kuncinya, …** — "the key is…". *Kunci* (key) is used exactly like the English metaphor. *Dengan begitu* ("that way, thereby") links a method to its result, and is a useful cohesion marker for your own writing section.

**Sangat Unggul pun bukan mimpi.** *Pun* after a noun means "even": *anak kecil pun tahu* (even a small child knows). Lestari switches from *Anda* to *Mbak Sarah* in the last line, and the warmth is deliberate: the lesson is over, the encouragement is personal.

grammars.title: The subjectless-sentence trap
body: Each wrong sentence below starts with a preposition that swallows the subject. Remove the preposition, or keep it and make the verb passive.
after: *Menurut Kepala Dinas mengatakan* is the most famous error of all, and it contains two ways of reporting at once. Choose one: *Menurut Kepala Dinas, jadwalnya berubah* or *Kepala Dinas mengatakan bahwa jadwalnya berubah*.
The test for a subject: ask *Siapa yang membahas?* If the only candidate sits behind a preposition, the sentence fails.

grammars.title: Redundancy the test loves
body: *Pleonasme* means saying the same thing twice. Speech is full of it and nobody minds; formal writing, and the UKBI, mind very much.
after: ⚠️ *Para* with a plural reduplication is the same mistake: *para guru-guru* should be *para guru* or *guru-guru*. You met this in Unit 2, and it still turns up in UKBI papers every year.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Hasilnya sudah keluar
dialogs.intro: Three weeks later, a Tuesday afternoon at the office. The results email has just arrived, and Yoga has noticed Sarah staring at her screen without clicking.

lines.text: Mbak, katanya hasil UKBI keluar hari ini?

lines.text: Iya, surelnya barusan masuk. Saya belum berani membukanya.

lines.text: Yaelah, Mbak. Buka aje. Kalau jelek, kita traktir bakso buat penghiburan.

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: Pantes aje tiap hari Mbak benerin tulisan saya. “Praktek” jadi “praktik”, “ijin” jadi “izin”.
lines.id: No wonder you correct my writing every day. “Praktek” becomes “praktik”, “ijin” becomes “izin”.

lines.text: Itu gara-gara Ibu Maria, Jar. Draf pertama kami dulu penuh coretan merah.
lines.id: That's Ibu Maria's doing. Our first draft back then was covered in red ink.

notes: **Hasilnya keluar** — results "come out", as in English. *Pengumuman* is the announcement; *lulus* (to pass) is not really used for the UKBI, because it grades everyone on a scale rather than passing or failing them.

**Surel** is the official Indonesian word for email, a blend of *surat elektronik*. Offices and letters use it; most people still say *email* (pronounced *i-mél*). Similar official blends: *unggah* (upload), *unduh* (download), *daring* (online, from *dalam jaringan*).

**Yaelah** — a Jakarta exclamation of mild impatience, "oh, come on". With *aje* and *buat* (for) instead of *untuk*, Fajar is at his most Betawi. *Penghiburan* (consolation) comes from *hibur*, to cheer up.

**Nggak nyampe segitu** — "don't reach that much". *Nyampe* is spoken *sampai*; *segitu* is spoken *sebegitu* (that much). The same set: *segini* (this much), *segitu* (that much), *seberapa?* (how much?).
**Pantes aje** — "no wonder", from *pantas* (fitting). Standard: *Pantas saja* or *Pantaslah*. It is how you react when a mystery is suddenly explained: *Pantas saja dia capek, semalam tidak tidur.*

**Kali ini saya yang traktir.** *Traktir* means to pay for someone else's food or drink, and taking turns to *traktir* is a pillar of office friendship. *Saya yang…* ("I'm the one who…") is the focus shape from B1 Unit 17, and it settles who pays with no argument.

grammars.title: Talking about a test
body: The words for results are easy to confuse. *Nilai* is a mark or grade, *skor* a numeric score, and *predikat* the named band a score falls into.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: I registered for the UKBI last month.
The test consists of five sections.
My highest mark was in the grammar section.

after: ⚠️ *Terdiri atas* and *terdiri dari* are both common; the language guides prefer *terdiri atas*. It is exactly the kind of distinction a *kaidah* question will test.

blocks.text: The UKBI is run by the Badan Pengembangan dan Pembinaan Bahasa (*Badan Bahasa*), the government language agency that also publishes KBBI. Civil servants, teachers, journalists and foreigners take it, usually in the computer-based adaptive version, *UKBI Adaptif*, where each question depends on how you answered the last.

head: Section
Name
What it tests
rows: understanding talks, news and dialogues, heard once
judging and correcting sentences, spelling and word forms
understanding and inferring from written texts
writing an organised text on a given topic
speaking on a topic, recorded and assessed

blocks.text: Sections I–III are multiple choice. Sections IV and V are marked by assessors on content, organisation, accuracy and register. For the writing section, remember Lestari's advice: two minutes for a *kerangka* (outline) pays for itself.
Scores run up to 800 and fall into seven named bands (*predikat*). The ranges below are those the Badan Bahasa has published; check the current guide before you book.

head: Predikat
Score
Roughly means
rows: exceptional; writes and speaks like an expert editor
superior; confident in complex formal tasks
intermediate; fine for most work, some slips

blocks.title: Words from the band names
items: *madya* — middle, intermediate: *ahli madya* (A.Md.) is the title of a three-year diploma graduate.
*semenjana* — middling, ordinary; a literary word you will rarely hear outside this scale.

blocks.text: Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
